title: Atonement
events_chronological: On a hot day in 1935, thirteen-year-old Briony Tallis finishes a play to be performed for her brother's homecoming.
Briony watches from an upstairs window as her sister Cecilia strips to her underwear and climbs into the fountain in front of Robbie Turner, the housekeeper's son.
Robbie drafts a letter of apology to Cecilia, sends the obscene version by mistake, and Briony reads it on the way.
Briony walks in on Robbie and Cecilia making love in the library and takes it for an assault.
The twins run off, and during the search Briony sees Lola being raped in the dark and names Robbie as the man.
Robbie is arrested and taken away in front of the family, and Cecilia breaks with all of them.
In 1940 Robbie is released from prison into the army and is separated from his unit in the retreat across France.
Cecilia, now a nurse in London, writes to Robbie, and the two spend a few hours together on his leave.
Robbie walks to Dunkirk with two corporals and reaches a beach of burning vehicles, shot horses and thousands of waiting men.
Robbie lies down in a cinema on the seafront and dies of septicaemia the night before the evacuation.
Briony, eighteen, takes a nursing place in London instead of Cambridge and treats men brought back from France.
Briony learns that Lola is marrying Paul Marshall, the man who actually raped her.
Briony goes to Cecilia's flat, finds Robbie there, and promises to recant her statement and set the truth down in writing.
Cecilia is killed when a bomb bursts the water main above Balham Underground station in October 1940.
In 1999 the elderly Briony, dying and giving her last interview, admits that she never went to the flat and that Robbie and Cecilia never saw each other again.
Briony says she gave the two of them in her novel the life they were never allowed, and the film shows them together at the seaside cottage.
syuzhet_notes: The 1935 afternoon is told forward but partly doubled, with the fountain and the library replayed once as Briony misreads them and once as they happened. Told-order bullet 9 is a flashback to Robbie's leave, cut into the walk to Dunkirk. The film's largest displacement comes at bullets 13-16, where the closing interview establishes that bullet 12 never happened at all and that the lovers had already died apart, years before the scene the film has just shown.
fabula_notes: Most of the film is Briony's novel rather than the story world, and the ending cancels one scene outright; the chronology here follows what the interview establishes as true, which puts Robbie's and Cecilia's deaths before the flat scene the film depicts. The seaside cottage is explicitly named as an invention.
